name: Asthma
definition: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways characterized by variable and recurring symptoms, reversible airflow obstruction, and bronchospasm. The airways become inflamed, narrow, and produce excess mucus, making breathing difficult. Asthma affects people of all ages but often starts in childhood. Triggers include allergens, respiratory infections, exercise, cold air, air pollutants, and stress. The condition ranges from mild intermittent to severe persistent, significantly impacting quality of life if not properly managed.
symptoms: Coughing (especially at night or early morning)
Difficulty sleeping due to breathing problems
Inability to speak in full sentences (severe attacks)
causes: Allergens (dust mites, pollen, pet dander, mold)
treatments: Daily controller medications to prevent symptoms
Quick-relief rescue inhalers for acute symptoms
Asthma action plan development with healthcare provider
Regular monitoring with peak flow meter
Patient education on proper inhaler technique
prevention: Keep home clean and free of allergens
Use air purifiers with HEPA filters
Avoid tobacco smoke and secondhand smoke
prognosis: Asthma is a chronic condition that cannot be cured but can be effectively controlled with proper treatment. Most people with asthma can lead normal, active lives with appropriate management. Well-controlled asthma has minimal symptoms, rare exacerbations, and normal lung function. Poorly controlled asthma can lead to permanent airway remodeling, reduced lung function, and life-threatening attacks. Children may outgrow asthma, but it can return in adulthood. Severe asthma affects about 5-10% of patients and may require advanced therapies.

name: Hypertension
definition: Hypertension, commonly known as high blood pressure, is a chronic medical condition in which the blood pressure in the arteries is persistently elevated. Blood pressure is measured as systolic (pressure during heartbeat) over diastolic (pressure between beats). Normal blood pressure is below 120/80 mmHg. Hypertension is defined as blood pressure consistently at or above 130/80 mmHg. Often called the 'silent killer' because it typically has no symptoms until significant damage has occurred to the heart, blood vessels, kidneys, and other organs. It is a major risk factor for heart disease, stroke, kidney disease, and other serious conditions.
symptoms: Pounding in chest, neck, or ears
causes: Primary/essential hypertension (no identifiable cause, 90-95% of cases)
Certain medications (NSAIDs, decongestants, birth control pills)
testsAndProcedures: Blood tests (kidney function, cholesterol, blood sugar, potassium)
CT or MRI of adrenal glands (if secondary cause suspected)
medications: Angiotensin II receptor blockers (losartan, valsartan, olmesartan)
treatments: DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension)
Sodium restriction (less than 2,300 mg/day, ideally 1,500 mg)
Regular aerobic exercise (150 minutes/week moderate intensity)
prevention: Heart-healthy diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains
prognosis: Hypertension is a lifelong condition that requires ongoing management. With proper treatment and lifestyle modifications, blood pressure can be effectively controlled, significantly reducing the risk of complications. Uncontrolled hypertension leads to serious complications including heart attack, stroke, heart failure, kidney disease, vision loss, sexual dysfunction, and peripheral artery disease. Target blood pressure varies by individual risk factors but generally aims for less than 130/80 mmHg. Medication adherence is crucial as stopping treatment causes blood pressure to rise again. Regular monitoring and follow-up are essential for optimal outcomes.

name: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
definition: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by high blood sugar levels resulting from insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency. Unlike Type 1 diabetes, the pancreas still produces insulin, but the body's cells do not respond effectively to it (insulin resistance), and over time, insulin production may decrease. This leads to elevated blood glucose levels that, if uncontrolled, cause damage to blood vessels, nerves, and organs throughout the body. Type 2 diabetes accounts for 90-95% of all diabetes cases and is strongly associated with obesity, sedentary lifestyle, and genetic factors.
symptoms: Numbness or tingling in hands or feet
causes: Poor diet (high in processed foods, sugar, unhealthy fats)
Ethnicity (higher risk in African Americans, Hispanics, Native Americans, Asian Americans)
treatments: Medical nutrition therapy and carbohydrate counting
Weight management and loss if overweight
prevention: Healthy diet rich in fiber, whole grains, fruits, vegetables
Limit processed foods and added sugars
prognosis: Type 2 diabetes is a progressive condition that requires lifelong management. With proper treatment, blood sugar can be well-controlled, and complications can be prevented or delayed. Uncontrolled diabetes leads to serious complications including cardiovascular disease (heart attack, stroke), nephropathy (kidney disease), retinopathy (vision loss), neuropathy (nerve damage), foot problems (ulcers, amputations), and increased infection risk. Some patients achieve remission through significant weight loss and lifestyle changes. Life expectancy is reduced by 6-7 years on average compared to non-diabetics, but this gap narrows with good glycemic control. Regular monitoring and comprehensive care are essential.

name: Major Depressive Disorder
definition: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), commonly known as clinical depression, is a serious mental health condition characterized by persistent feelings of sadness, hopelessness, and loss of interest in activities once enjoyed. It affects how a person thinks, feels, and handles daily activities such as sleeping, eating, and working. Depression is more than just feeling sad or going through a rough patch; it is a real medical condition that requires understanding and treatment. MDD can occur at any age but often begins in adulthood. It is one of the most common mental disorders and a leading cause of disability worldwide.
symptoms: Persistent sad, anxious, or empty mood
Loss of interest or pleasure in activities (anhedonia)
Feelings of guilt, worthlessness, or helplessness
Difficulty concentrating, remembering, or making decisions
Physical symptoms (headaches, digestive problems, chronic pain)
causes: Brain chemistry imbalances (neurotransmitters: serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine)
Stressful life events (trauma, loss, relationship problems)
testsAndProcedures: Physical examination to rule out medical causes
Blood tests (thyroid function, vitamin levels, complete blood count)
Review of medical and family history
medications: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs): fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram, paroxetine, citalopram
Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs): venlafaxine, duloxetine, desvenlafaxine
treatments: Combination of medication and psychotherapy (most effective)
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) for severe or treatment-resistant cases
Hospitalization for severe cases or suicidal ideation
prevention: Continuation of treatment to prevent relapse
prognosis: Major Depressive Disorder is highly treatable, with 80-90% of people eventually responding well to treatment. However, it is often a recurrent condition; about 50% of people who recover from a first episode will have one or more additional episodes. Without treatment, episodes typically last 6-12 months. With treatment, most people improve within 4-8 weeks. Risk of recurrence increases with each episode. Chronic depression can lead to significant disability, relationship problems, substance abuse, and increased risk of suicide. Early treatment, medication adherence, and ongoing therapy reduce recurrence risk. Approximately 10-30% of patients have treatment-resistant depression requiring alternative approaches.

name: Osteoarthritis
definition: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis, a degenerative joint disease characterized by the breakdown of cartilage—the protective tissue covering the ends of bones in joints. As cartilage deteriorates, bones begin to rub against each other, causing pain, stiffness, and loss of movement. OA most commonly affects the hands, knees, hips, and spine. Unlike inflammatory arthritis, OA is primarily a wear-and-tear condition, though inflammation plays a role in its progression. It develops gradually over years and is a leading cause of disability in older adults.
symptoms: Joint pain (worse with activity, better with rest)
Joint stiffness (especially in the morning or after inactivity)
Tenderness when pressing on the joint
Loss of flexibility and range of motion
Grating sensation or crepitus during movement
Bone spurs (hard lumps around the joint)
Difficulty with daily activities (walking, climbing stairs, gripping objects)
causes: Gender (more common in women after menopause)
Other types of arthritis (rheumatoid arthritis, gout)
testsAndProcedures: X-rays (show cartilage loss, bone spurs, joint space narrowing)
MRI (detailed images of cartilage and soft tissues)
Blood tests (to rule out other types of arthritis)
Assessment of functional status and pain levels
medications: Tramadol (for severe pain when other options fail)
treatments: Assistive devices (canes, walkers, braces, shoe inserts)
prevention: Stay physically active with low-impact exercises
Use proper body mechanics and posture
prognosis: Osteoarthritis is a chronic, progressive condition with no cure. However, symptoms can be effectively managed with appropriate treatment. Progression varies widely; some people have mild symptoms that remain stable, while others experience significant deterioration. Early intervention and lifestyle modifications can slow progression and maintain function. Severe OA may require joint replacement surgery, which has high success rates (90% of knee and hip replacements last 15-20 years). Quality of life can be maintained with proper management. Complications include chronic pain, disability, sleep disturbances, depression, and reduced mobility.
